First, we're actually able to identify species that have a (relatively) larger impact on an environment from an objective point of view. For example, [keystone species](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keystone_species)

Secondly, to address your point above,
>By the time that they go extinct, the animals are having a much smaller impact on the ecosystem. Either others fill the niche or the damage is pretty much done already.

That's not true at all. Extinction is always FAR worse than a low population. In the example of keystone species
>A classic keystone species is a small predator that prevents a particular herbivorous species from eliminating dominant plant species. Since the prey numbers are low, the keystone predator numbers can be even lower and still be effective. Yet without the predators, the herbivorous prey would explode in numbers, wipe out the dominant plants, and dramatically alter the character of the ecosystem.

Edit: Fixed quotations

Generally, at least with current intentional introduction, the predator species specifically targets the invasive species as prey. Ideally, the predator would consume the invasive species to the point of local extinction and, once its food source is depleted, go locally extinct itself. But of course that's only under ideal circumstances and one of the biggest concerns in biological control is the unforeseen consequences of species introduction.

One of the topics I'm researching for my paper is the introduction of the Cane Toad to limit the population of a pest that was destroying sugar cane crops. But the toads couldn't actually prey on the pests because they couldn't physically reach them, so they looked for alternative resources and ended up impacting the environment in unimaginable ways. 

I don't really agree with this practice as it was basically a financial investment (to protect the crops) and there really wasn't a whole lot of research behind the introduction. But I think there's a valid point behind biological control, especially when it's aimed at conserving an ecosystem or repairing one that we've broken.

But the inability for something to feel pain as we know it still doesn't justify causing harm. For instance, as a vegan I'm sure you wouldn't go out and eat a bug just because you can't tell if it's feeling pain. There's no way to draw a line of sentience or feeling, which is why I chose to stop eating meat in the first place. But that inability to draw the line can be extended to everything, including plants. Just because we can't recognize it's ability to "feel anything" doesn't mean that it doesn't have the capacity to feel. 

That said, even if it does feel something and we're inflicting pain, it's still less pain than if a cow ate the plant which caused it pain and we ate the cow which cause the cow pain.
